passage: It was forty-two degrees on election day, and the queue outside the school booth snaked round the playground. Sahil, twenty-five, had spent two evenings reading the candidates' records on the election commission's site and comparing their promises about the ward's water supply. Ahead of him, his neighbour Dolma-la, seventy and slow on the stairs, was fanning herself with a newspaper. Sahil gave her his umbrella and his water bottle, then walked her to the shade to wait until her turn came. After voting he went straight to the community kitchen near the market, where he'd volunteered every Sunday for a year. He didn't talk about big ideas much. He just kept showing up.

qa.q: What did Sahil give Dolma-la?
qa.a: His umbrella and his water bottle.

qa.q: What does Sahil spending two evenings on the candidates' records suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he feels real concern for the ward and wants to choose thoughtfully, not just vote out of habit.

qa.q: Which of Sahil's choices show his values working in everyday life?
qa.a: Reading the records before voting, helping Dolma-la in the heat and volunteering every Sunday show care turned into small, steady actions.

qa.q: How might Dolma-la see Sahil?
qa.a: Dolma-la probably sees him as a kind, dependable neighbour who noticed her struggling in the heat and quietly helped.

grounding: An adult turns concern for others into steady local acts: thoughtful voting, volunteering and helping a neighbour.

passage: Every Saturday morning, Avni's small living room in the Pune flat filled with children: the watchman's two sons, the girls whose mothers cooked in the building, a boy from the Somali family on the fifth floor. Avni, twenty-four, taught them English with picture cards and bad jokes. Her flatmate Kashish watched from the kitchen door. Avni greeted the sweeper, Ramesh-bhau, by name every morning, always asked after his knee, and had signed up to help at the ward's polling booth next month. "You never post about any of this," Kashish said. Avni shrugged, sorting crayons. "It's not a speech. It's just Saturday." Kashish found herself picking up a stack of cards to help.

qa.q: What did Avni use to teach the children English?
qa.a: Picture cards and bad jokes.

qa.q: Why might Avni say 'It's just Saturday'?
qa.a: Avni feels content and at ease with the teaching as a normal part of her week, not something to show off or a grand act.

qa.q: What small steady acts show Avni's concern for everyone around her?
qa.a: She teaches children from many backgrounds, greets the sweeper by name and asks about his knee, and volunteers at the polling booth.

qa.q: How is Kashish affected by watching Avni?
qa.a: Kashish seems to admire her and is quietly moved to join in, picking up the cards to help.

grounding: An adult puts wide concern into action through weekly teaching, respect for neighbours from all backgrounds and civic volunteering.

passage: "Sunday again, Vijay? The ward clean-up?" Sarita asked from the sofa. "Yes, didi. Want to come?" "You and your causes. What difference does a lane make?" "The drain by the school floods every monsoon because of plastic. Last year the little kids waded through it." Sarita put her phone down. "And the new family upstairs? You carried their gas cylinder." "They'd just moved from Manipur. They didn't know anyone." "You also read all those ward candidate lists before voting." "Somebody should." Vijay tied his shoes. "I can't fix the world, didi. I can fix our lane and say hello." Sarita sighed and reached for her chappals. "Fine. One hour. Show me this drain."

qa.q: Why does the drain by the school flood every monsoon?
qa.a: Because of plastic.

qa.q: What does Vijay mean when he says he can't fix the world?
qa.a: He believes big problems are too large for one person, but feels small, steady acts like cleaning the lane and welcoming neighbours are worth doing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation with Sarita?
qa.a: When Vijay explained the flooding drain and the little kids wading through it, Sarita saw the local reason and chose to join him.

qa.q: How does Sarita view Vijay's causes at first?
qa.a: Sarita is sceptical at first, doubting a lane makes any difference, but becomes curious enough to come along.

grounding: A sibling dialogue shows an adult turning broad concern into small, regular local acts that win over his sister.

passage:
I'm Bhupen, twenty-five, and when I look back at the year before last, I laugh at myself a little. I was a young man with strong opinions about everything: climate, equality, how the country should be run. I posted long threads at midnight. I didn't know the name of the woman who swept our lane.
Then Alka, a friend from college, asked if I'd teach at the night school for adult learners near the Guwahati railway colony. Two evenings a week, Assamese and basic maths, for security guards and cooks. I said yes mostly to be polite.
It changed me more than any thread. I learned that Jonali, who sweeps our lane, wants to read her grandson's school reports. I started going to our ward meetings. Before voting, I actually read what the candidates had done, not just their slogans. I began greeting the new family downstairs properly.
The ideals didn't go away. They just started living in my week.

qa.q: Who does Bhupen teach at the night school?
qa.a: Security guards and cooks.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel now when he remembers his midnight threads?
qa.a: He feels a little amused at himself, seeing that he held big ideals but knew little about the people right around him.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Bhupen lives his values?
qa.a: Saying yes to Alka's request to teach at the night school, which led him to learn Jonali's name and hopes and take part in local life.

qa.q: How might Jonali experience Bhupen's change?
qa.a: Jonali now has someone who knows her name and her wish to read her grandson's reports, instead of a young man who never noticed her.

grounding: It shows an adult who turns big ideals into local action by teaching at a night school, attending ward meetings, voting thoughtfully and greeting neighbours of every background.

passage:
Volunteer note, Thursday. Chandrika, coordinator, community food bank, Amritsar.
Amandeep (26) has come every Thursday for eight months, straight from his office. What I notice is how he treats people. He learns names. He greets the elderly widower, the young migrant labourers, the student who is embarrassed to be in the queue, all the same way: eye contact, a joke, no hurry.
Last month, when a volunteer made a crude remark about one family's language, Amandeep said calmly, "Everyone here gets the same respect," and moved on to stacking rice.
On election day he took the morning off and came in the afternoon, and told me he'd spent the week reading about the local candidates. He talks less about big causes than some others, but he never misses a shift.
Next: I will ask him to help train new volunteers.

qa.q: How long has Amandeep been coming to the food bank?
qa.a: Every Thursday for eight months.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's calm reply to the crude remark suggest about his values?
qa.a: It suggests he truly believes every person deserves equal respect, and cares more about living that value than making a scene.

qa.q: Why is Chandrika's plan to have Amandeep train new volunteers a good choice?
qa.a: His steady, respectful habits are exactly what new volunteers need to learn, so his example can spread.

qa.q: How might the student who is embarrassed to be in the queue experience Amandeep?
qa.a: The student probably feels less ashamed, being greeted by name with the same warmth as everyone else.

grounding: It shows an adult who volunteers steadily, votes after reading about candidates and treats people from every background with the same respect, turning wide concern into local action.
